Other Primes

Number TheoryDivisibilityRiemann Hypothesis
Game: Find the numbers that never show up in a big table, and see why they are the primes.
How to play: Pick any cell to see where it comes from, switch between the two views, and make the table bigger.

Look for the math

The sieve of Eratosthenes crosses out composites step by step. This table writes them all down at once, and the primes are what is left over.

A multiplication table in disguise

Row i (counting from 0) starts at 4 + 3i and grows by 3 + 2i, so the cell in row i, column j holds n = 4 + 3i + j(3 + 2i). Then x = 2n + 1 = (2i + 3)(2j + 3): the "Show x" view is the multiplication table of the odd numbers 3, 5, 7, … Row one lists the odd multiples of 3 (from 9), row two those of 5 (from 15), and so on.

Why the theorem holds

An odd x > 2 is composite exactly when it is a product of two odd numbers that are both at least 3, which is exactly when it sits in the "x" table. So x is prime exactly when n = (x − 1) / 2 is missing from the "n" table. The logic test checked this against trial division for every odd x a 30 × 30 table can decide. A table only holds products of odd numbers up to 2·size + 1, so a small table can miss a big composite such as 3 × 101 = 303; it never wrongly rules out a prime.

Why this matters for primes

Counting the holes in the table is counting primes. The holes thin out in an irregular but statistical way, and how irregular is what the Riemann Hypothesis is about.

Make the table 30 × 30 in the "n" view and look for the biggest gaps between missing numbers.
